items.title: Opposition parties Pro and Volt team up to force budget deal
items.summary: Opposition parties Pro and Volt have joined forces for the next round of budget negotiations as they try to step...
items.body_text:
Opposition parties Pro and Volt team up to force budget deal
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
Opposition parties Pro and Volt have joined forces for the next round of budget negotiations as they try to step up the pressure on the cabinet to make further concessions on social security.
Prime minister Rob Jetten said ministers had spent the last week drawing up “a new and attractive offer” addressing opposition parties’ concerns on welfare, the cost of living and replacing the “Box 3” asset tax mechanism.
Pro leader Jesse Klaver said the combined votes of his left-wing party and the pro-European Volt would give the government a “stable majority” in both houses of parliament.
An agreement with both Pro and Volt would give the coalition parties a comfortable majority in the lower house and the 16 seats it needs in the Senate, where Pro is the largest group but still needs Volt’s two seats to get over the line.
But the right-wing liberal VVD, the party of finance minister Eelco Heinen, is anxious not to make too many concessions to Pro, which would risk driving its voters away to its rivals such as JA21 and Geert Wilders’ far-right PVV.
Pick a side
“We are fighting for progress for ordinary people and a fair contribution from the super-rich,” Klaver said. “We believe in progressive co-operation.”
Volt leader Laurens Dassen said: “The world is changing rapidly. People expect politicians to work together towards a sustainable and innovative future.”
Jetten has been under pressure from the opposition on left and right to choose a side after all parties poured cold water on his hopes of finding a route through the middle.
The prime minister argued he would be “short-changing the country” if he excluded one side from the talks, but JA21 leader Joost Eerdmans said a broad approach “isn’t going to work” while Klaver warned his party would block the entire budget if the cabinet tried to do separate deals for each department.
Welfare cuts
Heinen has already agreed to postpone or cancel around half of the €6 billion cuts to welfare spending that were in the coalition agreement in February, but Pro wants the cabinet to go further.
Parties such as JA21, on the other hand, want to see even bigger welfare cuts, arguing that lower taxes are the best way to relieve the pressure on households and businesses.
Jetten and Heinen held talks on Saturday with Pro, Volt and the ChristenUnie, whose leader, Mirjam Bikker, said there had been “movement” from the coalition parties.
The ChristenUnie’s priorities are to ensure households are able to pay for essentials through the winter as energy and grocery bills rise. Bikker said it was “high time” that the coalition parties “feel the urgency” to make a deal.
BBB back on board
Later on Saturday the two ministers are due to talk to JA21 and the orthodox-protestant SGP, who have formed a right-wing alliance with 12 seats in the lower house.
Jetten and Heinen will also speak to Jan Struijs, leader of pensioners’ party 50Plus, and Henk Vermeer of the farmers’ party BBB, who are the second largest party in the Senate.
Jetten had initially said the BBB were no longer an option after the party backed a motion of no confidence during the budget debate, but he and Vermeer patched up their differences in a phone call last week.

items.body_text:
Man shot dead in packed bar in Amsterdam was prison warden
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
A man who was shot dead on a packed terrace in Amsterdam on Friday afternoon was a warden at a local prison, Dutch media have confirmed.
Marcel Blijd was killed at point-blank range as he sat outside De Baanderij restaurant on the NSDM quay, on the north bank of the IJ, in what initially appeared to be a row over a dog running off its leash.
Sources quoted by Het Parool and local crime news sites said the gunman had previously been detained in Zaandstad prison, where Blijd worked, but it is not clear if the two men knew each other.
The shooting at 3pm was witnessed by dozens of people who were enjoying a drink at the bar, and filmed by several people in the area.
Video footage showed the gunman, wearing a white shirt and red trousers, threw the weapon into the water but made no effort to flee and surrendered to police when they arrived a few minutes later.
 One witness said the two men clashed initially over the shooter’s dog, which was running loose around the quayside and barking. “He walked up and down a few times. We thought they were going to come to blows, but then there were shots.”
An ambulance and air ambulance were called to the scene, but Blijd could not be saved. A child’s buggy was parked next to the spot where he lay.
Detectives are now investigating whether the shooting was linked to Blijd’s position at Zaanstad jail, where some of Amsterdam’s most dangerous criminals are housed, including members of the Top 600 – a list of repeat offenders, many with connections to the underworld.
“Father figure”
Blijd worked in the prison system for 30 years and was seen as a “father figure” by colleagues and the young criminals he worked with, one colleague told Het Parool.
“Marcel could get on with everybody,” the colleague said. “If you were working with him in the cell block, you knew it was going to be a good day.”
Police cordoned off the area around the terrace and ferries to and from Amsterdam Centraal Station, which dock beside the restaurant, were suspended for three hours while investigations were carried out at the scene.
Witnesses were taken in police vans to the local police station to have their statements taken. Anyone who was in the area at the time can contact Victim Support Netherlands (Slachtofferhulp) for advice and counselling.

items.body_text:
New group home for psychiatric patients tried in Rotterdam
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
Rotterdam is to set up a new type of supervised accommodation for homeless people with serious psychiatric problems and addiction issues.
Forty people will be brought together under one roof in Poortugaal, a village near Rotterdam that is also home to a forensic psychiatric clinic, in a supervised environment where they can receive more structured support.
The residents will be allowed to stay in the facility for up to eight years, receiving long-term and structured support that is often lacking in temporary accommodation.
Around 1,500 people in the Netherlands are classed as posing a high risk to public safety. They often have learning difficulties, suffer from psychiatric illness and struggle with addiction, which can lead to aggressive, disruptive or deranged behaviour in public.
Many of the patients have spent their lives alternating between living on the streets and being incarcerated in clinics or prisons, posing a danger to themselves and others.
Pillar to post
“They get passed from pillar to post when what they really need is intensive support for several years,” Laura van Goor, of Artes, the organisation running the facility, told Nieuwsuur. “But we don’t have that right now in the Netherlands.”
Psychiatric clinics are intended for short stays of around three months, but patients often end up staying longer to prevent them ending up back on the streets.
But the treatment is short-term and keeping patients in care for longer adds to waiting lists.
Van Goor said the patients would have more freedom to move around on the campus than in smaller-scale facilities, while also benefiting from a more structured regime. They will not be allowed out unsupervised.
Drink and drugs will be formally banned, unlike in temporary housing where usage is usually tolerated. “But it’s not a case of ‘if you use, you’re out,’ Van Good said. “That’s not possible: 95% of them have drug problems.”

items.title: Russia condemns Polish city’s “barbaric” removal of Monument of Gratitude to the Red Army
items.summary: The fate of the monument has been subject to a long-running legal and political battle in Rzeszów.
items.body_text:
Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work!
Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support.
Russia has criticised the removal of a monument in the Polish city of Rzeszów expressing “gratitude” to the Soviet Red Army. It called the move “barbaric” and “sacrilegious”.
The monument – part of which will be moved to a nearby Soviet cemetery and another to a museum – has been the subject of a long-running legal and political battle, amid wider debate in Poland about “decommunising” public spaces, especially in the wake of Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
⚡️Komentarz Ambasady Rosji w Polsce
23 września 2026 r. w Rzeszowie (województwo podkarpackie), decyzją władz polskich i z naruszeniem dokumentów rosyjsko-polskich dotyczących ochrony obiektów dziedzictwa memorialnego, rozpoczęto proces demontażu pomnika wdzięczności żołnierzom… pic.twitter.com/HYuNeLG5dy
— Russian Embassy, PL (@rusemb_pl) September 24, 2026
The Monument of Gratitude to the Red Army, standing 8.5 metres tall and weighing 6.6 tons, was erected in Rzeszów, southeast Poland, shortly after the end of World War Two, when the Soviets had pushed Nazi Germany out of Poland and then installed their own communist government.
It is located on Ghetto Victims Square, a public space also created after the war on the grounds of the city’s former Jewish cemetery, which had been destroyed by the German occupiers in 1942.
Poland’s Institute of National Remembrance, a state historical body, notes that the monument was erected just a few metres from where two Polish anti-communist resistance fighters who had been members of the wartime Home Army (AK) had been publicly hanged by the communists.
The monument’s plinth featured bas-relief sculptures depicting Red Army Generals Ivan Konev and Karol Świerczewski, soldiers, and industrial and agricultural workers carrying a hammer and sickle. At the top of the 8.5-metre column was a statue of a woman and child.
In 2016, the then-ruling national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS) government introduced a law requiring local authorities to “decommunise” public spaces by removing objects and names that “propagate communism”. That triggered a legal battle in over the monument in Rzeszów.
The government-appointed provincial governor and the Institute of National Remembrance (IPN), a state historical body, moved to have it dismantled, arguing that the monument glorified communism.
But city hall – led by left-wing mayor Tadeusz Ferenc, who had been a member of the communist party before 1989 – challenged the decision. It argued that the monument did not promote communism and noted that its name, referring to gratitude to the Red Army, was not an official one.
In 2019, the provincial administrative court sided with the city and overturned the decision to remove the monument.
However, Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022 prompted many Polish municipalities that had not removed Soviet-era monuments to begin doing so.
In April 2022, Rzeszów’s current mayor, Konrad Fijołek, announced that his city’s monument would be removed from its current location and placed in a Soviet soldiers’ cemetery elsewhere in the city.
“In principle, I am not in favor of dismantling or demolishing monuments, as they are a testament to history,” said the mayor. “But in light of the current wartime reality, this monument should not remain in its current location. But we are not barbarians; we will not demolish the monument, but relocate it.”
However, the IPN opposed the idea of relocating the monument and refused to cover the costs of doing so. It wanted it to be liquidated entirely.
Another Soviet memorial has been demolished in Poland – the 43rd since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine.

items.title: Polish president “doesn’t like” Trump inviting Putin to G20 but will still attend summit
items.summary: "If it were up to us, Russia should be isolated in all international forums," says President Nawrocki's chief foreign policy aide.
items.body_text:
Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work!
Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support.
Polish President Karol Nawrocki “does not like” the fact that the Trump administration has invited Vladimir Putin to this year’s G20 summit in the United States, says his chief foreign policy aide.
However, Nawrocki, who is a close ally of Donald Trump, still plans to attend the event – which Poland has been invited to as a guest rather than a full G20 member – in order to represent Polish interests and push for full membership of the group.
🔴 "Nie podoba nam się to". Nawrocki ma problem po decyzji Trumpa
Prezydent Karol Nawrocki weźmie udział w grudniowym szczycie G20 w Miami, na który zaproszono również Władimira Putina. Szef Biura Polityki Międzynarodowej Kancelarii Prezydenta Marcin Przydacz przyznał na antenie…
— Wirtualna Polska (@wirtualnapolska) September 26, 2026
The G20, a major intergovernmental forum, holds an annual summit whose location rotates among members. This year’s event will take place in December at a golf resort in Miami owned by Trump.
On Wednesday this week, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio announced that Trump has invited Putin to attend the summit, saying that “we think it’s an opportunity for him to engage…with other world leaders” and “we hope that’s an invitation he’ll accept”.
“If you only meet with people that you agree with, then these are very nice meetings but nothing happens,” added Rubio. “In order to solve problems, you have to meet with people that you disagree with or the people that you might have some issues with.”
Marco Rubio on Russia:
We’ve invited President Putin to the G20. We think it’s an opportunity for him to engage not just with Trump, but with other world leaders.
We hope that’s an invitation he will accept. pic.twitter.com/e0GSz7Y8gm
— Clash Report (@clashreport) September 23, 2026
Last December, Rubio also announced Poland’s invitation to the summit as a guest, saying that it would be “assuming its rightful place in the G20”. In May this year, the US also “expressed its strong support for Poland’s accession to the G20 as a permanent member”.
Poland will be represented by Nawrocki, who is a vocal critic of Putin and Russia, and is himself on a Russian wanted list for his work leading efforts to demolish Soviet-era monuments in Poland.
In an interview on Sunday with news website Wirtualna Polska, the head of Nawrocki’s international policy office, Marcin Przydacz, was asked if the US was right to invite Putin. “We don’t like it,” he replied.
“But we were invited to the G20 summit as guests, and it’s not our role to tell the participants who should be part of it,” he added, noting that Russia is a founding member of the G20. However, “if it were up to us, Russia should be isolated in all international forums.”
Nevertheless, “President [Nawrocki] is going to Miami and doesn’t intend to change his plans at this stage”, confirmed Przydacz. “Poland will be at the G20 summit because it’s in our interest…This isn’t the only format in which we sit with countries we disagree with.”
However, he also added that, “if the Russian leader actually intends to come, and is not just invited, we will discuss this with our European and Euro-Atlantic allies”.
Putin has not attended a G20 summit in person since 2019, initially due to the COVID-19 pandemic and later amid the fallout from Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine and the International Criminal Court’s arrest warrant against him. The US is not a member of the ICC, so the arrest warrant does not apply on its territory.
Przydacz told Wirtualna Polska that Putin “should be held accountable for his crimes”. Asked if Nawrocki would shake hands with the Russian president at the G20, Przydacz said that he “doesn’t think any interactions will occur”.

items.summary: The decision adds to marital benefits now available in Poland to same-sex couples married elsewhere in the EU.
items.body_text:
Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work!
Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support.
The Polish government has granted same-sex couples who married abroad and have had their wedding certificates transcribed into the Polish registry the same tax rights as other married couples.
The decision follows a ruling by the Court of Justice of the European Union (CJEU) requiring Poland – whose domestic law does not allow same-sex couples to form any type of legal union – to recognise same-sex marriages contracted in other EU member states.
Podpisałem dziś interpretację ogólną, która zapewnia, że osoby, które uzyskały transkrypcję aktu małżeństwa będą miały w polskich urzędach skarbowych takie same prawa i obowiązki podatkowe jak wszyscy małżonkowie.
— Andrzej Domański (@Domanski_Andrz) September 24, 2026
“Today, I signed a general interpretation ensuring that persons who have obtained a transcription of their marriage certificate will have the same tax rights and obligations in Polish tax offices as all other married couples,” announced finance minister Andrzej Domański in a social media post.
A general interpretation is an official position taken by the finance ministry aiming to clarify the application of tax law in a specific area.
Among the benefits that couples with a transcribed foreign marriage certificate can now receive include preferential treatment under inheritance and gift tax rules and the ability to file joint personal income tax returns.
Couples may also pay tax on behalf of a spouse and refuse to testify as a witness in proceedings involving their spouse.
“This is about basic equality, justice and fairness,” Domański told broadcaster TVN. “We want these rights to be enforceable in an effective way.”
The finance minister said that the decision would have a “negligible” impact on the state budget. He also noted that such couples would be subject to the obligations that apply to other married couples in Poland, which include liability for their spouse’s tax obligations.
Osoby, które uzyskały tak zwaną transkrypcję aktu małżeństwa, będą miały przed polskimi urzędami skarbowymi dokładnie takie same prawa i obowiązki jak pozostali małżonkowie – powiedział minister finansów Andrzej Domański w rozmowie z Grzegorzem Kajdanowiczem w @faktypofaktach w… pic.twitter.com/uVwDaD3ZDk
— tvn24 (@tvn24) September 24, 2026
The finance minister’s decision has drawn criticism from right-wing politicians, who argue that recognition of same-sex marriage violates the constitution, which states that “marriage, being a union of a man and a woman, shall be placed under the protection and care of the Republic of Poland”.
Paweł Szefernaker, chief of staff to President Karol Nawrocki, who is aligned with the right-wing opposition, said Domański’s actions were “inconsistent with the constitution” and had been carried out “without legislation, without debate, without honestly telling Poles what is really happening”.
“Everyone has the right to a private life,” he added. “However, the state has a duty to protect the legal order and provide tax support for marriage.”
Patryk Jaki, a deputy leader of the national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS), Poland’s largest opposition party, said that the finance minister’s actions “clearly violate Polish law and will have legal implications in the future” for Domański, who is “writing additional points in the indictment against himself”.
Sławomir Mentzen, one of the leaders of the far-right Confederation (Konfederacja) group, said the tax interpretation “will be revoked on the very first day” if his party comes to power.

items.title: Survey: most employees handle personal matters during working hours
items.summary: A CV.ee survey shows that the strict line between working time and personal time has long blurred in many workplaces.
items.body_text:
Survey: most employees handle personal matters during working hours
A CV.ee survey shows that the strict line between working time and personal time has long blurred in many workplaces.
CV.ee job portal conducted a survey (link in Estonian) about how people use their working time. A little over a 1,000 people responded to the questionnaire.
The results showed that 76 percent of respondents deal with personal matters during working hours, said CV.ee's marketing and communications specialist Gertu Matikainen.
"For example, going to the doctor, taking a child to kindergarten, or handling some other unavoidable matter is not always possible to push outside working hours," Matikainen said. "And if an employee can arrange such obligations flexibly and work tasks are always completed, it may be a reasonable solution compared with strictly separating nine‑to‑five working time and the rest of life."
Company culture matters
Nearly three‑quarters of respondents use working time to visit a doctor or handle other health‑related errands. In addition, personal emails are sent and time is spent on social media, Matikainen noted.
The study shows that people themselves see this rather as situation‑based. 51 percent of respondents believe that handling personal matters during the workday should be approached according to the situation and also the company's culture.
Matikainen said that flexible work arrangements must have clear boundaries so that personal errands do not hinder the completion of work tasks. Such flexibility may in turn mean that people are willing to deal with work also in their free time. For example, slightly under half of respondents read work emails every day while on vacation.
For the employer, flexible work arrangements can be positive, because they give the employee the opportunity to organize their life better and may reduce daily stress. For example, an employee can go to the doctor or handle child‑related obligations without having to take a separate vacation day for each such matter.
What people are thinking
How much do you deal with personal matters during working hours at your job? Some answers by people on the streets of Tartu:
"Very minimally, working time is working time, in that sense I respect working time and I respect my company."
"For me there isn't really much difference between work and personal matters. My work is different, I don't go to work in the usual way."
"Sometimes there is time during work to handle some personal matters, for example to write an email or pay a bill."
Most common personal tasks done during working hours:
- Going to the doctor or handling health‑related errands (74%)
- Sending and/or reading personal emails (66%)
- Spending time on social media (41%)
- Planning trips or making bookings (28%)
- Child‑related errands (e.g., taking to kindergarten/school etc.) (24%)
- Going to the store (24%)
- Household chores, such as cleaning or repairs (22%)
- Shopping in online stores (22%)
Source: CV.ee survey
--
Editor: Argo Ideon
Source: ERR radio news

St. Nicholas' Church recreated in Lego after 18‑month fan effort
Enthusiast Nikolai Mordan's recent interest has been building Lego versions of well‑known Tallinn buildings.
"Most Lego enthusiasts start by buying Lego sets, building them and putting them on a shelf, then they think: what next?" said Mordan.
"After that they look online at how someone has built something and shared instructions with others, you buy the pieces or dismantle a set and rebuild it, then you have someone else's creation, and the next step is: what can I build myself."
Mordan got his first Lego in 1993. "My parents gave me a small Formula One car for Christmas."
he began pursuing the hobby more actively in 2011. "It's still going on," Mordan said, adding that he no longer keeps count of how many different Lego sets he has. "I lost track when there were about 1,000–1,500 pieces."
Nowadays Mordan is interested in building Estonian landmarks out of Lego. "Tallinn Town Hall was the first. I thought about what else I could take on and decided that maybe I should try doing something with St. Nicholas (Niguliste) Church," he said.
From the first idea of St. Nicholas to reaching the exhibition took a year and a half.
Mordan plans well‑known buildings using software; at the moment he is working on two buildings from Ülemiste City, for which the program helps calculate that the material cost — meaning Lego bricks — totals 400 euros.

items.title: Estonia to hold regular National Defense Council meetings
items.summary: Until now, the meetings of the National Defense Council have taken place ad hoc at the president's invitation, but the next Estonian president, Ülle Madise, wants to make the institution's work systematic, said future presidential adviser Taimar Peterkop.
items.body_text:
Estonia to hold regular National Defense Council meetings
Until now, the meetings of the National Defense Council have taken place ad hoc at the president's invitation, but the next Estonian president, Ülle Madise, wants to make the institution's work systematic, said future presidential adviser Taimar Peterkop.
Madise aims to organize regular meetings of the National Defense Council and, after taking office, will hire former Secretary of State Peterkop as the Council's adviser.
"I am very pleased that Taimar Peterkop agreed to take on the substantive preparation and organization of the National Defense Council's work. Taimar Peterkop knows broad‑based national defense both theoretically and practically, understands the importance of dignified human relations and of forward‑looking, determined and persistent joint action," Madise said in a press release.
According to the Constitution of Estonia, the President of the Republic is the highest leader of national defense, and the National Defense Council is an advisory body to the president.
The council provides an opportunity to bring together representatives of the president, parliament, government and defense forces to discuss national defense issues and helps shape a comprehensive view of the country's security.
"Times and circumstances require greater attention from those responsible for security so that confidence prevails in society. National defense means not only military defense but also the development of broad‑based national defense, and therefore I see the need to make the council's work more regular and consistent. Involving an adviser will help organize the council's work better and more substantively," Madise noted.
"I greatly appreciate the invitation from the future president to join her team. In this role I can apply my knowledge and experience in preparing for crises and resolving them, and thereby contribute to Estonia's ability to withstand crises in a tense geopolitical environment," Peterkop said in the press release.
Peterkop served as Secretary of State from 2018 to 2025 and before that, from 2015 to 2018, as Director General of the Information System Authority (RIA). Previously he worked at the Ministry of Defense as deputy permanent secretary and as a defense policy adviser at the Estonian Embassy in Washington. Peterkop currently works at the e‑Governance Academy as a senior expert in cybersecurity.
Peterkop graduated from the University of Tartu Faculty of Law and earned a master's degree in strategic leadership from the U.S. Army War College.
Estonia's next president Ülle Madise will take office on 12 October, giving the oath before the Riigikogu.
--
Editor: Mait Ots, Argo Ideon

items.title: Bosnia Court Blocks Republika Srpska From Funding Secessionist Lobbying
items.summary: Court bans Republika Srpska from paying international lobbying firms to promote the entity’s independence from the Bosnian state.
items.body_text:
Bosnia Court Blocks Republika Srpska From Funding Secessionist Lobbying
Bosnian lawmaker Denis Zvizdic, who initiated teh legal challenge. Photo: EPA/FELIPE TRUEBA.
Bosnia’s Constitutional Court on Friday declared that budgetary funds used by Bosnia’s Serb-dominated Republika Srpska entity to pay foreign consulting firms to lobby for independence violate the state’s constitutional architecture.
The ruling targets a consulting agreement signed between the Republika Srpska Representative Office in Vienna and a Montreal-based firm, Dickens & Madson Canada Inc., which listed “the independence of Republika Srpska” as a core political objective.
The legal challenge was initiated in April by a state-level lawmaker, Denis Zvizdic, who argued that using taxpayers’ funds to lobby against Bosnia’s sovereignty and territorial integrity was unconstitutional.
A 2008 ruling allowed the entity to engage foreign firms for general economic promotion. However, the court has now established that funding campaigns explicitly promoting secession represents an assault on the constitutional order.
“The Constitutional Court hereby prohibits all payments from the budget of Republika Srpska regarding the consulting services contract concluded with Dickens & Madson Canada Inc.,” the court said. “Financing lobbying services for goals that run counter to the Constitution of Bosnia and Herzegovina is strictly incompatible with the constitutional order.”
The applicant, Zvizdic, welcomed the announcement, saying the entity had weaponised massive public funds for anti-state campaigns.
“Public money cannot be used to finance lobbying aimed against the state of Bosnia and Herzegovina, its territorial integrity, sovereignty and its institutions,” Zvizdic stated.
“This binding decision establishes a clear legal standard: citizens’ money must serve development and investment, not the undermining of the state,” he added.
Under Bosnia’s state-level laws, entities possess no constitutional right to unilateral secession. Furthermore, ignoring or violating a binding order of the Constitutional Court carries severe penalties.
The court said the full text of the judicial decision will be delivered to all parties and published on its official website within the month.

items.title: Week in Review: Spyware, AI and Arrests
items.summary: Tech concerns mount over elections in Serbia, spy chief’s arrest tests Albania’s NATO ties, protests over court verdicts continue in Kosovo and North Macedonia mulls impact of dangerous virus, our selection of Balkan Insight’s Premium stories this week shows.
items.body_text:
Week in Review: Spyware, AI and Arrests
Damaging arrest
Albania’s State Intelligence Service chief, Vlora Hyseni, was arrested and suspended for allegedly revealing state secrets and assisting an offender. While members of the ruling Socialist Party insists that any wrongdoing was on her part, the opposition again raised questions about her appointment to a top position. For the NATO member country, issues surrounding the integrity and reputation of the State Intelligence Service could undermine cooperation with the alliance, experts warned.
Read more: Albanian Spy Chief’s Arrest a Major Blow to NATO Member’s Reputation (September 24, 2026)
Spyware allegations
The student movement in Serbia has become the biggest opponent to the current government under President Aleksandar Vucic. Expectations are now on early parliamentary elections scheduled for October 25. But just a month before the polls, Serbia’s institutions have failed to address allegations that student protesters, politicians and activists were targeted with Pegasus, an advanced, military-grade spyware that can target devices remotely.
Read more: Serbian Authorities Ridicule Spyware Attack Allegations Before Elections (September 24, 2026)
AI misuse
Misuse of AI has already been seen in Albania during the ongoing anti-government “Flamingo Revolution” protests, and BIRN has identified many cases in which AI was used to disseminate false information that was then amplified through anonymous social media pages and accounts. As the country prepares for local elections in 2027, concerns are growing over the legislative gaps and limited technical capacity to address the misuse of AI in democratic processes.
Read more: Albania ‘Not Ready for the Risks’ as AI Enters the Electoral Arena (September 23, 2026)
Sentence protests
The verdict convicting Hashim Thaci, Jakup Krasniqi, Kadri Veseli, and Rexhep Selimi sparked protests in Pristina, gathering thousands in the streets of Kosovo’s capital. The Kosovo Specialist Chambers in The Hague convicted the four former Kosovo Liberation Army, KLA, leaders of war crimes last week, sentencing them to 25, 25, 18 and 13 years in prison, respectively. Protesters see the verdict as an injustice, while the parliamentary group of the Democratic Party of Kosovo, PDK, announced it was pushing for a change to the law underpinning the Hague court.
Read more: ‘Our War is Being Judged’: In Kosovo, Outrage at Hague Verdict Simmers
New Balkan realities
Experts say the geopolitical situation is changing dramatically, as Russia loses its capacity to shape and influence politics in the Western Balkans and the United States changes its role in international relations. In an opinion piece for Balkan Insight, Nikola Xaviereff, a Research Fellow at the German Council on Foreign Relations Centre for Order and Governance in Eastern Europe, Russia, and Central Asia, predicts that the Western Balkans “will align to the zeitgeist of transactionalism with both liberal and authoritarian powers”.
Read more: As Geopolitical Competition Intensifies, the EU’s Balkans Policy Must Adapt
Escalating virus
West Nile virus has hit Southern and Southeastern Europe this summer, with climate change seen as a big contributing factor. Cases in North Macedonia reached their highest level this year, with at least eight confirmed deaths. The situation has revealed that the country lacks targeted, updated measures to monitor, mitigate and prevent health issues related to the virus.
Read more: West Nile Cases Escalate in North Macedonia, Spurring Calls for Action (September 21, 2026)
Speaker’s journey
Montenegro’s parliament failed to debate a motion to dismiss Andrija Mandic of the right-wing New Serbian Democracy party as speaker because there was no quorum to hold the session. The motion came after Mandic sent a message of condolence to the son of the former Bosnian Serb military commander and genocide convict Ratko Mladic following his recent death.

items.title: ARTE Europe Weekly: Datacentres and Hidden Cost of Digital Progress
items.summary: Seen as energy guzzlers and environmental polluters, datacentres are facing growing opposition across Europe.
items.body_text:
The drive for more data storage and processing capacity in Europe is fuelling protest across parts of the continent. Their energy demands, environmental impact and effects on nearby residents are often behind the opposition. But demand is set to soar as AI development supercharges their expansion, with the EU aiming to at least triple its data centre capacity by the end of the decade. Industry insiders and experts argue Europe needs the drive to ensure its digital sovereignty, and remain competitive globally. But with considerable concerns, is it time to put the brakes on?
This programme is produced by the European platform ARTE and available in 10 languages through the European media partnership BEAM. The hub is coordinated by ARTE and includes Balkan Insight (BIRN), Sinopsis (BIRN Romania), El País (ES), Gazeta Wyborcza (PL), Internazionale (IT), Ir, (LV), Kathimerini (GR), Le Soir (BE) and Telex (HU). The partnership receives EU-funding following DG CNECT’s call for European Media Hubs within the framework of the EU’s Multimedia Actions.

Soldiers from several units of the Hungarian Defense Forces successfully completed their first jumps with packed air-cell parachutes following their round-canopy training exercises.
As part of their basic training with packed air-cell parachutes, they carried out the exercise from an altitude of approximately 1,200 meters at the Szolnok-Szandaszőlős sports airfield. This moment marks a particularly important professional milestone for paratroopers.
Until now, those who completed the course had performed their tasks with tied-canopy parachutes, but from now on, they will be soaring through the skies using the air-cell technique!
Our paras can now perform their jumps from a variety of state-of-the-art aircraft. Either from the Hungarian Air Force’s French-made Airbus H225M helicopters, or from their brand new Embraer KC-390 transport aircraft.

items.title: Star Authors Expected at the 31st Budapest International Book Festival
items.summary: The 31st Budapest International Book Festival, taking place at a new venue—the Hungexpo Budapest Congress and Exhibition Center—from October 1–4, welcomes the public with nearly 200 events and 400 book signings. At Thursday’s press conference presenting the program, Katalin Gál, president of the Hungarian Association of Book Publishers and Distributors, said that it is a […] The post Star Authors Expected at the 31st Budapest International Book Festival appeared first on Hungary Today.
items.body_text:
The 13th edition of the Kecskemét exhibition brings together 146 works and series by 147 artists.Continue reading
The 31st Budapest International Book Festival, taking place at a new venue—the Hungexpo Budapest Congress and Exhibition Center—from October 1–4, welcomes the public with nearly 200 events and 400 book signings.
At Thursday’s press conference presenting the program, Katalin Gál, president of the Hungarian Association of Book Publishers and Distributors, said that it is a tradition for the festival to showcase the culture, literature, and book publishing of a single country or region, but this year, in an exceptional move, three countries— Germany, Austria, and Switzerland—and contemporary German-language literature will receive special attention.
She noted that
this year’s guest of honor at the festival is Colm Tóibín, a world-renowned author of contemporary Irish literature, who will also receive the Budapest Grand Prize. His new book, The Magician, will also be published in Hungarian for the festival, and to mark the 50th anniversary of the establishment of Irish-Hungarian diplomatic relations, Irish literature will play a prominent role at the festival.
The festival will present the György Somlyó Literary Translation Award, established in 2025 by the French Institute in Hungary, which aims to encourage the younger generation to translate from French into Hungarian.
In addition to Hungarian creators, nearly one hundred foreign writers will be waiting for the audience at the festival; there will also be spaces and events designed for children, and comics will feature prominently in the program. Next year, Finland and Finnish literature will be featured as guests of honor.
Alexander Renggli, the Swiss ambassador, noted at the press conference that this year marks the 80th anniversary of the reestablishment of Swiss-Hungarian diplomatic relations, which had been severed during World War II. As he explained, three writers from Switzerland will be attending the book festival: Nelio Biedermann, Melinda Nadj Abonji (Melinda Nagy Abonyi), and Christian Kracht. The first two have close ties to Hungary, while the latter—best known for his novel Eurotrash—is one of the most well-known Swiss authors in Hungary, she explained.
Miriam Bruns, director of the Goethe-Institut Budapest, mentioned that among the German authors appearing at the festival will be Martina Hefter, with her book Good Morning, How Are You?, and Eugen Ruge, who will present his book Pompeii: Five Speeches by Jovna. Fabian Ortner, director of the Austrian Cultural Forum, said that among others, Tonio Schachinger will read from his novel Real Times, and Dimitré Dinev will read from his work The Age of the Brave.
Featured Image: Facebook/Budapesti Nemzetközi Könyvfesztivál/International Book Festival Budapest

items.body_text:
Dining Guide recognized outstanding talents and pioneering concepts in Hungary.Continue reading
Hungary is marking World Tourism Day with a series of special programs across the country, as Visit Hungary and Tourinform offices invite visitors to discover the country’s diverse natural, cultural, and architectural attractions through nearly 100 events.
From September 21 to 30, Tourinform offices across the country are inviting visitors to participate in themed city tours and a variety of programs.
The initiative also aims to promote the concept of sustainable tourism, while drawing the attention of domestic travelers and the local population to the natural, cultural, and architectural treasures of Hungary’s destinations.
In Balatonfüred on September 27, participants in the “The Grapes Are Ripening” tour will wind their way through the vineyards of Balatonfüred and Aszófő, enjoying a wine tasting in a unique setting. In Badacsony on this day, a guided wine tour brings the experience of hiking closer to the local wine culture and the personal world of the winemakers. In Vonyarcvashegy, a guided forest and wine-tasting tour invites visitors on a pleasant walk where history and local flavors come together.
Mystery lovers can embark on unique adventures in several cities.
On September 27, urban legends will come to life during a city-exploration walk in Veszprém, while an exciting treasure hunt awaits visitors in Tihany. In Zalaegerszeg, the “Green Maze” detective adventure game promises an unforgettable experience.
You can experience time travel all across the country. In Bükfürdő, the history of the healing waters comes to life during an interactive, nature-filled walk; in Szarvas, an unconventional tour of the town lets you travel back in time from a whole new perspective; and in Szombathely, the “Giant Board Game” adventure invites you on an exciting historical journey dating back to ancient times.
World Tourism Day offers a variety of opportunities centered on experiences, community programs, and discovery—whether it is wine-tasting events, thrilling mysteries, or even time travel.
Via Turizmus.com; Featured photo: Pexels

items.title: Úgy érzem, elraboltak. Minden olyan jogot megsértettek, ami az életben létezik, mivel emberi lények vagyunk
items.summary: Trump migránsellenes politikájának egyik csúcsa, hogy sokszor instabil, nyomorgó, autoriter harmadik országokba deportál bevándorlókat. Olyanokat, akik olykor bírósági védelem alatt állnak, és egyik napról a másikra tudják meg, hogy Közép-Afrikába vagy Szváziföldre toloncolják ki őket.
items.body_text:
Úgy érzem, elraboltak. Minden olyan jogot megsértettek, ami az életben létezik, mivel emberi lények vagyunk
„Csak pár órával a repülőút előtt jöttem rá, hogy Afrikába fognak deportálni. Senki sem figyelmeztetett, véletlenül jöttem rá, amikor sikerült megnéznem a nevem az emberek listáján, akiket Libériába szállítanának, egy országba, amiről sosem hallottam ezelőtt. Nem volt időm jogilag megvédenem magam vagy elbúcsúznom a családomtól. Nem tudtam tenni semmit, már mindent eldöntöttek” – mondta egy névtelen, csak C.-ként azonosított venezuelai férfi a spanyol El Paísnak. C.-t is feltették augusztus 19-én egy gépre, ami a louisianai Alexandriából a nyugat-afrikai Libériába vitte, sok más sorstársához hasonlóan, akarata ellenére.
C. 2021-ig a venezuelai hegyekben élt, majd a romló biztonsági és gazdasági helyzet elől, életét féltve menekült az Egyesült Államokba. Tavaly decemberben vették őrizetbe, holott a státusza is rendben volt, rendőrségi ügyekbe se keveredett. Azt mondták, két hétig tartják bent, de nyolc hónap lett belőle. Koszos, patkányokkal teli őrizeti központokban volt, és még a gyereke születésekor se lehetett jelen, ezután röptették váratlanul egy kontinenssel arrébb.
A venezuelai A. is azt mondta, hogy hosszas őrizetben eltöltött idő után őt is felrakták egy repülőre. Nem akart fölszállni, de az ICE-ügynökök azt mondták neki, akár erővel is felteszik. „Amint elfoglaltuk a helyünket, mind könnyekben törtünk ki. Összeláncolt kezekkel és lábakkal utaztunk az egész úton”, ami 15 órán át tartott – derült ki az El País cikkéből.
A. szerint elszakították a családjától, most fél, hogy a feleségét is elviszi az idegenrendészet, az ICE, a lánya a történtek miatt pszichológushoz jár. Azt mondta, már nem is akarna visszamenni az USA-ba, inkább családostul Európába települne. Annyi pozitívumot elmondott, hogy Libériában kedvesen fogadták őket, az elhelyezésükre kijelölt szálloda is tiszta volt, és szabadon mozoghatnak.
Libéria korlátos szabadsága
Brazilok, kolumbiaiak, guatemalaiak, hondurasiak, venezuelaiak tengődnek most egy isten háta mögötti libériai hotelben. Furcsa történet az övék, jól megmutatja a Donald Trump amerikai kormánya által forszírozott bevándorláspolitika abszurd oldalát. Az amerikai kormány ugyanis megállapodásokat kötött harmadik országokkal arról, hogy az illegálisan az Egyesült Államokba belépett bevándorlókat hozzájuk toloncolhatják ki.
Részben pénzügyi támogatás fejében teszik ezt, de az amerikai kormány vámokkal és a segélyek felfüggesztésével is megfenyegetett több országot. A Marshall városában lévő hotelbe is zömmel olyanokat szállítottak, akik életükben nem jártak Afrikában, bár kameruniak és eritreaiak is ide kerültek a Libériába látogató CBS szerint.
Helyszíni interjúik alapján arról írtak, hogy sok kitoloncolt bevándorló családja az Egyesült Államokban maradt. Most sokuk hontalannak számít, nem tudja, mit csináljon, hova menjen, származási országába nem mer visszatérni, mert üldöztetéstől tart. „Aggódom. Úgy érzem, messze, a világ másik végén vagyok” – mondta a hondurasi Elvis Rodríguez Venturas a CBS-nek. Neki négy gyereke – köztük kettő amerikai állampolgár – és a felesége van Texasban, akik várják haza. Hondurasba nem küldhették vissza, egy bíró megakadályozta, mondván, hogy ott bántódása eshet.
Több bevándorló azt mondta a CBS stábjának, hogy bíróságokon nyertek pereket a kormányzat ellen, ezért nem küldhették vissza őket latin-amerikai hazájukba. Erre találta ki a Trump-kormány, hogy akkor máshova deportál. A kiutasítottak azt mondták, az ICE nem tájékoztatta őket arról, hova kerülnek, fellebbezésnek nem volt helye. items.summary: Több embert is letartóztattak robbanóanyaggal kapcsolatos bűncselekmények gyanújával.
items.body_text:
Robbanószereket keresnek a brit Fairford katonai bázisnál, egy környékbeli települést evakuáltak
A Gloucestershire megyei rendőrség közlése szerint több férfit letartóztattak robbanóanyaggal kapcsolatos bűncselekmények gyanújával az angliai RAF Fairford légibázis közelében. A helyszínen a brit hadsereg speciális tűzszerész egysége dolgozik, és több járművet is átvizsgált. A közeli Whelford település lakóit evakuálták, és egy szabadidőközpontba szállították őket, amíg a vizsgálatok folytatódnak.
A BBC azt írta, hogy az incidens kivizsgálását a brit terrorelhárítás vezeti. Tristan Wilkinson, a Cotswold kerületi tanács képviselője a BBC-nek nyilatkozva arra kérte az embereket, hogy maradjanak nyugodtak. Szerinte ez egy új fejlemény, ezért a találgatásokat a lehető legalacsonyabb szinten kell tartani. Wes Streeting brit védelmi miniszter pedig közölte, hogy kezelik az ügyet.
A brit királyi légierő (RAF) fairfordi támaszpontját régóta használja az Egyesült Államok előretolt műveleti bázisként. Március elsején Keir Starmer volt brit miniszterelnök azt is engedélyezte az amerikaiaknak, hogy a bázisról hajtsanak végre „védelmi” műveleteket az iráni rakétatelepek ellen. Az amerikai légierő a fairfordi incidensre reagálva arról számolt be, hogy az ott szolgáló személyi állomány „továbbra is éber”.
Az iráni Forradalmi Gárda még júliusban arra figyelmeztette Nagy-Britanniát, hogy ne engedélyezze az amerikai bombázók felszállását a fairfordi bázisról. Válaszul Nagy-Britannia kijelentette, hogy fegyveres erői készen állnak az ország megvédésére bármilyen támadással szemben.
items.normalised_title: robbanószereket keresnek a brit fairford katonai bázisnál egy környékbeli települést evakuáltak

Mellkason szúrta egy apa a fiát Győrben, a férfi belehalt a sérülésbe
A rendőrség közleménye szerint egy családi vita vezethetett ahhoz a bűncselekményhez, amelyben egy férfi mellkason szúrta a fiát egy konyhakéssel Győrben. Az áldozat olyan súlyos sérüléseket szenvedett, hogy a kórházba szállítása után életét vesztette.
A Győr-Moson-Sopron Vármegyei Rendőr-főkapitánysághoz szombat este 19 óra után érkezett bejelentés arról, hogy a győri Kossuth Lajos utca egyik lakásába egy férfit késsel megszúrta. A helyszínre érkező egységek a gyanúsítottat elfogták, majd a kihallgatása után őrizetbe vették, és kezdeményezték a letartóztatását. Az eset körülményeit, a Győr-Moson-Sopron Vármegyei Rendőr-főkapitányság Bűnügyi Osztálya büntetőeljárás keretén belül, szakértők bevonásával vizsgálja.

items.body_text:
Bolt and Lucid Plan 25,000 Autonomous Vehicles Across Europe
Prague Morning
Bolt and U.S. electric vehicle maker Lucid Group have announced a partnership to develop autonomous mobility services in Europe, with plans to deploy more than 25,000 fully autonomous vehicles across European cities over the coming years.
The vehicles will be based on Lucid’s upcoming Midsize platform and use NVIDIA Hyperion, a reference architecture and development platform for autonomous vehicles.
The companies plan to develop the vehicles for SAE Level 4 autonomous driving, which allows vehicles to operate without human control within defined conditions.
Bolt says the project is part of its wider ambition to have 100,000 autonomous vehicles operating on its platform by 2035.
The companies will work together from the early stages of vehicle development. Bolt will contribute traffic and mobility data, operational experience and knowledge of European markets, while Lucid will provide its software-defined vehicle platform and automotive technology.
Bolt will also define requirements covering the vehicle, software, safety and passenger experience. Its autonomous driving division will oversee the partnership and develop the infrastructure needed to operate the fleet.
This will include vehicle dispatch, charging, maintenance, remote assistance and customer support. Bolt also plans to own and operate the autonomous vehicles itself.
Rollout will depend on local regulations
The companies have not yet announced which European cities will receive the service first.
Bolt and Lucid said launches will take place city by city and depend on local regulations, official approvals and operational readiness. The companies also plan to work with autonomous driving technology providers, European regulators and policymakers before introducing the service.
For the foreseeable future, autonomous vehicles on the Bolt platform will operate alongside vehicles driven by human drivers.
Lucid’s side of the project will be led by Lucid Technologies, a newly established division bringing together artificial intelligence, advanced driver-assistance systems, autonomous driving and other digital technologies.
Bolt currently operates in more than 850 cities across 50 countries and says its platform serves more than 200 million customers. Its services include ride-hailing, car-sharing, electric scooters and food and grocery delivery.
Lucid Group, listed on the Nasdaq under the ticker LCID, develops electric vehicles and related technologies. The company operates manufacturing facilities in Arizona and Saudi Arabia.

items.body_text:
Prague Airport Works to Speed Up Border Checks for Non-EU Travellers
Prague Morning
Prague Airport and the Czech Ministry of the Interior are preparing additional measures to reduce waiting times for passengers arriving from non-Schengen countries following the introduction of the EU Entry/Exit System (EES).
The new system has made border checks more complex, particularly for travellers from outside the EU. Prague Airport says it has already introduced several measures aimed at keeping passenger flows moving during busy periods.
Airport staff, known as the Red Team, are assisting passengers in the terminal, directing them through the new procedures and providing information where needed. The airport has also adjusted passenger flow corridors based on data collected since the system was introduced.
One of the main issues identified so far is the self-service registration process. According to the airport, a significant number of passengers do not complete their registration at the kiosks, which can lead to additional delays at passport control.
Prague Airport is therefore examining the entire journey from the registration kiosks to passport control and looking at ways to make the process easier, particularly for families and older passengers.
“Data has shown us that the most common delays occur when people interrupt the registration process at the terminals,” said Radomír Lašák, Chairman of the Board of Prague Airport. “Together with the Police of the Czech Republic, we are not merely putting together temporary stopgaps but are redesigning the entire process so that it remains resilient even during peak periods.”
Further measures are also being prepared at the European level, including the possibility of allowing passengers to complete parts of the EES registration before departure. Airlines could also provide passengers with information about the process during flights.
The Czech Ministry of the Interior and the Immigration Police are working with Prague Airport on the next steps and have committed additional resources to help manage the new system.
Interior Minister Lubomír Metnar said the authorities’ priority was to maintain security standards while limiting the impact of the new procedures on passengers.
The airport said it will continue monitoring passenger flows and adjusting its procedures based on actual operations, particularly during peak travel periods.

items.body_text:
Czech Statehood Day 2026: What Is Open and What to Do in Prague
Prague Morning
September 28 is a public holiday in the Czech Republic, marking Czech Statehood Day and the feast of St. Wenceslas. This year, the holiday falls on a Monday, giving many people a three-day weekend.
For anyone planning to spend the day in Prague, however, there are two practical questions: which shops will be open, and what can you do around the city?
Where you can shop on September 28
Under Czech legislation regulating retail opening hours, shops with a sales area of more than 200 square meters must close on September 28.
The restriction applies throughout the day and covers large supermarkets, hypermarkets and home improvement stores.
Smaller shops with sales areas of up to 200 square meters are exempt and can open at their owners’ discretion. Petrol stations and pharmacies can also operate.
Other exceptions include shops located at airports, railway stations and bus terminals, as well as retail outlets inside healthcare facilities.
Why September 28 is Czech Statehood Day
The holiday commemorates Prince Wenceslas, a member of the Přemyslid dynasty who became one of the central figures in Czech history.
Wenceslas was killed by his brother Boleslav I on September 28, 935, in Stará Boleslav. His death later became the foundation of a cult that developed around him from the late 10th century onward.
His remains were transferred to Prague in 938 on Boleslav’s orders and buried in the Rotunda of St. Vitus. The reasons behind the transfer are not known with certainty, but the move helped strengthen Wenceslas’s status as a religious figure while also reinforcing Prague’s position as the center of the emerging Czech state.
Over the following centuries, Wenceslas became the patron saint of the Czech lands and an important symbol of Czech statehood.
The connection between Wenceslas and Czech political tradition was further strengthened under Charles IV, who commissioned the Crown of Saint Wenceslas. The crown became one of the principal symbols of the Czech monarchy and remains part of the Czech Crown Jewels.
See the Czech Crown Jewels at Prague Castle
September 28 is also the final day of this year’s exhibition of the Czech Crown Jewels at Prague Castle.
The jewels are being displayed in Vladislav Hall as part of the exhibition Habsburgs 500. Admission is free, and the display also includes a coronation robe dating from 1653 and other historical objects.
The exhibition closes at the end of the day on September 28.
Government buildings open to visitors
Several normally restricted buildings will also be accessible to the public.
Straka Academy, the official seat of the Czech government, will open its doors on September 28. Visitors can see the government meeting room, ceremonial areas and the building’s garden.
The program also includes an interactive exhibition called Journey of the Republic. Tours are free and begin at 10 a.m., with the final group scheduled to leave at 5 p.m.
The Ministry of Finance on Letenská Street will also welcome visitors. Tours start at 9:30 a.m. and include the ministry’s historic premises and the former monastery.
Museums and other attractions
The National Technical Museum in Letná will remain open on September 28, giving visitors access to its permanent exhibitions.
The Postal Museum will also be open.
For those looking for a more traditional Prague attraction, September 28 will be the final chance this year to ride the historic Letná Carousel.
Another option is the National Museum, where the Přemyslids exhibition examines the history of the dynasty that ruled the Czech lands during the country’s early medieval period.
The exhibition runs until October 15, 2026, making the public holiday particularly relevant for visitors interested in the history behind Czech Statehood Day.

items.body_text:
Georgia Marks 33 Years Since Fall of Sokhumi
National flags were lowered to half-mast at government buildings as Georgia commemorates the 33rd anniversary of the fall of Sokhumi on September 27, 1993, which ended the 1992–93 armed conflict in Abkhazia.
The date is associated with Tbilisi’s loss of control over the region and the ethnic cleansing of the Georgian population, resulting in the displacement of hundreds of thousands.
Among those who paid tribute at the Heroes Memorial in Tbilisi were Georgian Dream government officials, opposition representatives, and members of the diplomatic community. A march organized by the Abkhaz Council movement and joined by opposition parties and protest groups is planned later in the day from Tbilisi State University campus to the memorial to commemorate the day.
“September 27 is an utterly tragic day that reminds us of the gravity of the Abkhazia war. On this day, we commemorate the heroes fallen in Abkhazia and pay tribute to their heroic deeds and memory,” Georgian Dream Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze said. “It is our duty to do our utmost to restore the territorial integrity by peaceful means,” he added, noting that this was the dream of the Abkhazia war heroes.
Among those who paid tribute was also Courtney Austrian, the newly-appointed U.S. Chargé d’Affaires in Georgia. “We join our Georgian partners in remembering the sacrifice and courage of those who gave their lives to protect the Georgian homeland and those who have since been displaced after the war,” the U.S. Embassy wrote on X.
Tbilisi dispatched troops to the Autonomous Republic of Abkhazia in the summer of 1992 with the stated aim to protect the Abkhazia section of the Russian-Georgian railway.
The government troops were forced to withdraw from the region in September 1993, following the attack on Sokhumi on September 16, 1993, by Abkhaz militants and mercenaries from the Russian Federation. The attack occurred in violation of the July 27 ceasefire that envisaged the withdrawal of heavy Georgian weaponry from Sokhumi and its surroundings.
September 27 is associated in Georgia with the loss of control over Abkhazia and the ethnic cleansing of the ethnic Georgian population. An estimated 12,000 people were killed during the 13-month armed conflict, while more than 200,000 ethnic Georgians were displaced from the region.
Following the 2008 Russo-Georgian war, Moscow recognized Abkhazia as an independent state, but the region’s international recognition remains limited, with Nauru recently becoming the latest country to withdraw its recognition.

items.body_text:
Who’s Who in Georgian Party Politics? A Guide to the Party Landscape in 2026
Georgia’s party system is unusually difficult to map. More than 200 parties are formally registered, although many are inactive, while new parties, movements, and electoral alliances appear frequently. Parties split, rebrand, or cooperate for a single election and then separate again. For the outside observers, the formal party list therefore says little about which actors actually matter and how they relate to one another.
Author: Sandro Tabatadze, Assistant Professor, Tbilisi State University, Georgia
For much of the period after 2012, Georgian politics was organised around two poles: Georgian Dream–Democratic Georgia (GD), in power since 2012, and the United National Movement (UNM), which governed from 2004 to 2012 and then became the principal opposition force. That structure still matters, but it no longer captures the landscape as a whole. Many current parties emerged through splits from either GD or the UNM. While some continue to gravitate back toward one of these two poles, especially ahead of elections, others are becoming increasingly alienated from them. And then, there are forces that deliberately present themselves as alternatives to both.
Ideology alone is therefore a poor guide. Organisational origin, leadership networks and attitudes toward former and current ruling parties often explain behaviour better than conventional left–right labels. Foreign-policy orientation is another major dividing line, particularly the contrast between Euro-Atlantic integration and neutrality or openly Eurosceptic positions.
A third dimension has become more important since the disputed 2024 parliamentary election: institutional strategy. Most opposition parties rejected the results and refused to take up their mandates; some also boycotted the 2025 local elections, while others returned to electoral competition. Parliamentary representation alone is therefore no longer a reliable guide to political relevance.
How this guide classifies parties
This guide primarily focuses on political genealogy, but uses two more criteria, including foreign-policy orientation and current institutional strategy. Genealogy and foreign-policy position provide the main structure; participation in or boycott of elections and representative institutions helps distinguish parties within the same broader camp. While some forces and movements, including the Federalists, Girchi/Party of Free People, Girchi-More Freedom, Movement for Social Democracy, and Eurosceptic parties, maintain a strong ideological focus, such forces are yet to reach a share that would allow for an ideology-based classification of the entire political spectrum.
The categories are analytical rather than formal coalition labels: actors placed in the same group do not necessarily cooperate or share identical programmes. The guide covers 22 relatively visible political actors and divides them into five groups:
- The ruling and ruling-aligned camp
- The pro-European opposition originating from the ruling party
- Pro-European parties originating from the former ruling party and its splits
- Pro-European “third force” opposition
- The Eurosceptic opposition
1. The Ruling and Ruling-Aligned Camp
The ruling camp is centred on Georgian Dream (GD). Founded in 2012 by billionaire Bidzina Ivanishvili, now the party’s honorary chairman, GD came to power at the head of a broad opposition coalition. Over time, coalition government gave way to single-party rule. The party’s initial big-tent and broadly pro-Western profile has also changed substantially. GD still formally presents European integration as a national objective, but increasingly frames relations with EU institutions and Western partners through sovereignty, external interference and conspiracy narratives, including references to a “Global War Party” or “Deep State”. Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze currently chairs the party.

items.body_text:
Suspect With ‘Nazi-Fascist’ Group Links Detained Over Abuse of Minors
Georgia’s Interior Ministry said it detained a suspect with links to a “Nazi-fascist” ideology who had previously been convicted and was serving a suspended sentence, over two episodes of ill-treatment of minors. The accused faces up to 10 years in prison if convicted.
The ministry said in a September 25 statement that in 2023, “one of the leaders of a group with a ‘Nazi-fascist’ ideology, together with fellow group members, lured an acquaintance to an abandoned area in Tbilisi under false pretenses,” where they assaulted the minor with various “blunt objects” and subjected him to “inhuman and degrading treatment.”
The ministry did not specify whether the detainee was the leader of the group or one of its members.
The investigation further established that in 2025, the suspect organized the group assault and degrading and inhuman treatment of another minor, the ministry said.
It added that the probe revealed that the “accused’s associates filmed, on a mobile phone, video footage depicting the physical and psychological coercion and degrading acts committed against the minor, with the intention of posting it online.”
The suspect was detained following “complex investigative and procedural actions” and based on a judge’s ruling, according to the ministry.
“Some of the individuals involved in these crimes are already serving their sentences in a penitentiary institution,” the ministry said, adding that investigative actions are ongoing to identify other individuals connected to violent groups holding fascist ideology.
The ministry did not disclose the detainee’s identity. However, RFE/RL’s Georgian service reported that the person detained is reportedly Davit Japarov.
Georgian police have arrested at least 15 minors in recent months, including in January and March, on allegations of involvement in “neo-Nazi” and “radical fascist” groups that physically and psychologically abused people of various ages, including minors, with “extreme cruelty.”

items.title: Nine-year-old girl allegedly abducted in Ingushetia in retaliation for bride kidnapping
items.summary: According to local outlet Fortanga, the girl was held for around two weeks after her family ‘kidnapped’ a bride.
items.body_text:
A group of people allegedly abducted a nine-year-old girl in the village of Ali-Yurt in Ingushetia’s Nazran district in an apparent attempt to take revenge on the relatives of a man who had previously ‘kidnapped’ a bride, the local independent media outlet Fortanga has reported. The publication did not disclose the names of those involved, citing ethical considerations.
According to Fortanga, in early September, a man from Ingushetia abducted a woman to marry her. The woman’s father demanded that the young man’s relatives return her; they claimed they didn’t know where the two were.
The woman’s relatives then allegedly decided to take revenge, Fortanga wrote. Around two weeks after the alleged kidnapping, a group of unidentified people purportedly broke into the home of the perpetrator’s brother. The man himself was not at home. According to a source cited by Fortanga, the attackers broke down the door and found his wife, two young children, and a nine-year-old niece there. They allegedly abducted the girl and drove away.
According to Fortanga, she was returned after around two weeks and only after a criminal investigation was opened. The young man’s brother allegedly then withdrew his proposal to the woman’s family.
Fortanga says the relatives decided to make the story public because they fear that those who abducted the girl could avoid criminal prosecution.
There have been no official reports from law enforcement agencies in Ingushetia about the abduction.
The abduction of women and girls for the purpose of marriage has repeatedly led to conflict between relatives in the North Caucasus. The region has seen both staged abductions, in which young people act with the woman’s consent, and violent abductions carried out against her will.
The majority of cases do not go to court, but authorities have investigated some in recent years. In January 2023, police in Ingushetia searched for a 37-year-old man suspected of abducting a 16-year-old girl whom he allegedly intended to marry.
According to research by the human rights project AD REM, more than 650 reports of abductions for the purpose of forced marriage were registered in the North Caucasus between 1999 and 2007. Criminal cases were opened in roughly a quarter of those cases. Researchers note that there is no current statistics on such crimes and that many women do not report them to the police because they fear social stigma.
Among the reasons abducted women may not return home, according to Russian independent media outlet Mediazona, is the belief that a woman is considered ‘tainted’ after staying in a man’s home. Mediazona has published accounts from women who experienced forced marriages and noted that in some cases relatives refused to take abducted women back. One participant in the research, a woman from Chechnya, said that six of her cousins had been abducted and that none of them had been allowed by their older relatives to return home.
Similar cases have also occurred in Ingushetia. In 2009, 18-year-old Zaira Bopkhoeva was abducted for a second time. She had previously been abducted when she was under 16. According to Mediazona, she was subsequently considered ‘tainted’ and married her abductor. The marriage ended and she returned home. After the second abduction, her father’s relatives took her to a forest, beat her, and forced her to marry her abductor. In 2018, the European Court of Human Rights awarded Bopkhoeva’s mother €20,000 ($22,800) in compensation because the Russian authorities failed to investigate the circumstances of the case.
Ingushetia also has informal measures aimed at preventing bride abductions. In 2013, religious leaders in the republic introduced a fine of ₽200,000 ($2,300) for abducting a bride and ₽100,000 ($1,200) for each accomplice. Under Russian law, there is no specific charge for bride kidnapping.

items.title: Georgian Church trades barbs with Azerbaijan government over church excavations
items.summary: Azerbaijan’s Foreign Ministry warned the Georgian Church not to repeat the ‘well-known approaches of the Armenian Church’.
items.body_text:
Georgian Church trades barbs with Azerbaijan government over church excavations
A spat has erupted between the Georgian Orthodox Church and the Azerbaijani government over reported works at and around a church in Azerbaijan near the border with Georgia.
In a statement on Thursday, the Patriarchate of the Georgian Orthodox Church warned that ‘any intervention carried out both inside the church itself and in the surrounding area is of particular concern’. The statement was accompanied by photographs showing excavations cordoned off with red-and-white tape.
‘This raises numerous questions, both about the unclear purpose of the works and the rehabilitation of a Georgian cultural heritage site without the agreement of the Georgian side’, the Patriarchate said.
The site in question is referred to by the Georgian Church as the Kurmukhi Church of St George. Azerbaijan refers to the site as the Kurmuk Temple, insisting the area was home to an ancient Caucasian Albanian temple.
In their statement, the Patriarchate said the Church was an important monument of ‘historical and spiritual heritage’ for Georgia and its Church.
In a harshly-worded response on Friday, Azerbaijan’s Foreign Ministry told Azerbaijani state-run news agency APA that it was ‘not advisable for the Georgian Patriarchate to repeat the well-known approaches of the Armenian Church and follow its path’.
They said the remarks from the Georgian Church ‘contradict’ the spirit of friendship and partnership between the two countries.
‘The presentation of geographical and historical toponyms located in the territory of Azerbaijan under other names is unacceptable’, the ministry reportedly said.
Mutual respect toward territorial integrity and sovereignty ‘constitutes an important foundation of the strategic partnership relations’, the statement said. ‘It is precisely in this regard that the Georgian Patriarchate’s approach containing territorial claims with respect to Azerbaijan’s territorial integrity and sovereignty is incomprehensible’.
‘It is important that religious institutions refrain from approaches that could harm the historical friendship and good-neighbourly relations formed over centuries between the peoples of Azerbaijan and Georgia’, the statement continued.
‘All historical, cultural and religious monuments existing in the territory of Azerbaijan are an integral part of the national heritage of the Azerbaijani people and the Azerbaijani state’, it concluded.
The Patriarchate’s statement on Thursday highlighted that images of the excavations had caused a ‘strong reaction and justified outrage’ from the public in Georgia, saying it ‘negatively affects our good, neighbourly relations and the strengthening of cooperation between the two neighbouring states and peoples’.
Photos purportedly showing the excavations at the church began circulating on Georgian social media about a week before the Patriarchate’s statement. However, it is unclear when the pits shown in the photos were dug, and when they were cordoned off.
On Wednesday, another photo also circulated — reportedly taken at the site — showing a fence and an Azerbaijani sign reading: ‘Attention: Archaeological excavations in progress. Entry prohibited’.
Noting that it had not been contacted by any Azerbaijani state agencies about the works, the Patriarchate stressed the ‘importance’ of establishing the nature of the works and urged Georgian state agencies to engage with the process:
‘We believe that only through timely and coordinated cooperation is it possible to properly protect and preserve the site of Georgian spiritual and cultural heritage’, they concluded.
The largely inactive church is located in Azerbaijan’s northern Gakh District, near the Georgia border. The Georgian Church considers it part of Georgia’s cultural heritage. Georgian delegations — including representatives of the Patriarchate, parliament, and government — have travelled there multiple times over the years to mark St George’s Day.

items.title: Azerbaijani opposition leader tells Aliyev: give me a life sentence, free women political prisoners
items.summary: Azerbaijani President Ilham Aliyev has yet to respond to imprisoned Azerbaijani Muslim Unity Movement chair Taleh Bagirzade’s offer.
items.body_text:
Azerbaijani opposition leader tells Aliyev: give me a life sentence, free women political prisoners
Imprisoned Azerbaijani Muslim Unity Movement chair Taleh Bagirzade has offered to accept a life sentence in exchange for releasing detained women journalists and religious adherents. He addressed his offer in a letter to the Azerbaijani President, stating that if Ilham Aliyev agreed, he would personally send a message of gratitude.
The Muslim Unity Movement is a religious and political movement in Azerbaijan founded by Bagirzade in 2015. The group advocates for religious freedom, social justice, and greater political participation.
In his letter to Aliyev, Bagirzade said he disagreed with what he described as Aliyev’s ‘unhealthy governance’ of Azerbaijan, which he said had continued for years.
‘Mr Aliyev! You know better than anyone that for years we have rightly voiced strong criticism against your government, which has ruled through oppression, and that we will never accept your unhealthy governance. Of course, we are fully prepared to pay the heavy price for this and have no complaints. However, considering some of the unpleasant events that have taken place in Azerbaijan recently, we thought that after many years we might be able to reach an agreement with you on one issue’, Bagirzade wrote.
As part of the proposed agreement, Bagirzade asked Aliyev to increase his prison sentence in exchange for the release of women prisoners, specifically journalists and religious adherents.
‘You would change my 20-year prison sentence to life imprisonment. At your order, you impose the harshest punishment on my two minor children; if you wish, we can add my other two minor children as well, and we will have no complaints about any of this. In return, our only request is that you release the brave journalists and veiled women whom you had imprisoned on fabricated charges solely because of their investigations and activities’, he wrote.
Bagirzade said he would send Aliyev a letter of thanks if the president released the women prisoners.
Bagirzade is currently serving a 20-year prison sentence after being convicted in 2017 of attempting to change Azerbaijan’s constitutional order, among other charges, all of which he denies. International human rights organisations recognise him as a political prisoner.
His two minor sons, Mahammadhasan and Mahammadhuseyn Bagirzade, have also recently faced criminal charges in connection with an alleged fight at a school in Baku that took place on 7 April.
According to the family, an argument broke out in the schoolyard where the teenagers studied after one of the older students used offensive language. Mahammadhuseyn Bagirzade tried to stop them, which escalated the situation. The argument later turned into a physical fight, the family said.
According to the family’s account, Mahammadhasan Bagirzade intervened after seeing his brother being beaten by two people. The family said that one person from the other side suffered a broken nose as a result of the incident.
The family believes the conflict was orchestrated as a threat against Taleh Bagirzade and his family.
